3. Bind a tile for one-tap access
Tap a slot below to bind a shortcut to it, or long press that tile in the shade to bind it right there. Tapping the tile then opens the file directly, with no extra step.

Android reads a quick settings tile icon from its manifest entry, so it cannot be swapped at runtime. That is why direct tiles use one of six fixed line icons. A direct tile does follow the shortcut bound to it, so renaming that shortcut renames the tile. The QuickBar panel tile is the one that gives you the full 100-icon library, plus fully custom names.

HyperOS blocks activity launches that come from the background, which is what a quick settings tile is. QuickBar routes every tile tap through the system so it keeps working with the app closed. If a tile still refuses to open anything, allow background pop-ups for QuickBar below, and keep QuickBar out of the battery saver whitelist restrictions.

Android gives apps no way to take a tile back out of the shade, so each tile below has a switch that does it for you: turn it off and the tile disappears from the control centre, turn it back on and it can be added again. Binding and naming are kept, so nothing is lost. You can also remove a tile the system way: pull the shade down, tap edit, then drag it out of the active row.
